description:
IO-TS Lab is a team of space enthusiasts from Computer Science, Mechanical Engineering, Astronomy, and Business, united by a passion for exploring the cosmos. We aim to build an interactive platform using SPHEREx data to help people discover moving celestial objects. Join us to turn innovative ideas into real scientific impact! 

We’re looking for passionate teammates skilled in web, Python, AI/ML, astronomy, data visualization, and UI/UX who love solving challenges and exploring space.
summary:
SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer a browser-based SPHEREx blink workbench that helps users investigate possible moving or variable objects in repeated infrared sky observations. Users search by coordinates, retrieve matching observations, and compare time-separated frames through an intuitive blink interface with metadata, quality warnings, and provenance.

The platform divides responsibilities clearly: the frontend provides search and visualization; the backend manages investigations, archive retrieval, downloads, storage, and product serving; and the science pipeline validates FITS data, applies quality masks, aligns frames with WCS, and produces exploratory comparison products. A difference image can reveal candidate changes, but the system explicitly labels unverified results and avoids unsupported claims.

By making archival SPHEREx data easier to explore, SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer lowers the barrier to systematic time-domain astronomy. Its transparent workflow supports responsible scientific investigation and future follow-up of interesting infrared sources.
details:
SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer is a browser-based astronomical exploration platform that helps users investigate potentially moving or variable objects through repeated infrared sky observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission.

Users enter sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), and the platform automatically searches for relevant repeated observations from the NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx archive.

The application follows this workflow:

  1. Coordinate Search: Users enter RA and Dec coordinates to identify a region of interest in the sky.
  2. Observation Discovery: The backend searches the SPHEREx archive for repeated observations covering the requested coordinates.
  3. Data Retrieval: Suitable astronomical image cutouts are downloaded in FITS format.
  4. Data Validation: The science pipeline checks FITS integrity, quality flags, metadata, invalid pixels, and observation compatibility.
  5. Image Alignment: Images are aligned using World Coordinate System (WCS) information to ensure meaningful comparisons.
  6. Image Processing: Comparable PNG frames are generated, along with diagnostic difference images when observations are suitable.
  7. Interactive Visualization: Users can play, pause, navigate between frames, adjust the time slider, and switch between original images and difference views.
  8. Scientific Review: Observation timestamps, detector information, units, warnings, validation status, and processing provenance are displayed.

The platform also includes an AI-assisted navigation system that helps users understand the interface and explore its functionalities. The AI assistant supports navigation and onboarding but does not replace scientific validation.

2. What benefits does the project have?

SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer provides several scientific and practical benefits:

  • Simplifies Astronomical Exploration: Makes complex SPHEREx archival data easier to access and investigate.
  • Automates Data Processing: Reduces the manual effort required for searching archives, downloading FITS files, validating observations, and preparing images.
  • Interactive Visualization: Provides an intuitive blink viewer for comparing repeated observations over time.
  • Flexible Exploration: Supports generic coordinate-based searches rather than limiting users to predefined astronomical targets.
  • Integrated Workflow: Combines observation discovery, data retrieval, scientific processing, visualization, and provenance in one platform.
  • Improved Data Reliability: Uses quality checks, compatibility validation, and WCS alignment to reduce misleading visual differences.
  • Scientific Transparency: Displays warnings, missing metadata, and processing information instead of making unsupported assumptions.
  • Reproducibility: Maintains investigation details, processing records, and generated products.
  • Accessibility: Makes time-domain infrared astronomy more approachable for students, researchers, and citizen scientists.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to make time-domain infrared astronomy more accessible, efficient, and reproducible.

Exploring repeated astronomical observations traditionally requires specialized knowledge and multiple tools for archive searching, FITS file handling, image alignment, and temporal comparison.

SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer brings these activities together into a single browser-based environment.

The project aims to:

  • Help researchers investigate repeated infrared observations more efficiently.
  • Enable students to gain practical experience with astronomical data.
  • Allow citizen scientists to explore changes in astronomical images.
  • Help identify potentially interesting moving or variable sources for further investigation.
  • Encourage reproducible scientific workflows through transparent metadata and provenance.
  • Reduce the technical barriers associated with exploring astronomical archives.

In the longer term, the platform could support large-scale searches, automated candidate ranking, collaborative investigations, multi-frame visualization, and integration with additional astronomical archives.

Importantly, the platform is designed for scientific exploration rather than automatic discovery claims. Visual changes are treated as potential candidates for follow-up, not confirmed detections.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project combines modern web technologies with scientific Python libraries and astronomical data services.

Programming Languages

  • Python: Backend development and astronomical data processing.
  • JavaScript: Browser-side interactions and frontend functionality.
  • HTML: Web application structure.
  • CSS: Interface styling and layout.

Scientific Libraries and Tools

  • Astropy: Astronomical data handling, FITS processing, and WCS operations.
  • NumPy: Numerical computations and image-array processing.
  • FITS: Standard astronomical image-data format.
  • WCS: Coordinate-based image alignment.
  • Image Reprojection Tools: Aligning observations into a common sky coordinate system.

Data Sources and Services

  • NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Archive.
  • TAP/SIA-based observation discovery.
  • IRSA cutout services.

Backend Technologies

  • Web API framework.
  • REST APIs.
  • Background job processing.
  • Investigation state management.
  • File storage and caching.
  • Product serving and error handling.

Frontend Technologies

  • Browser-based web interface.
  • Interactive blink viewer.
  • Time slider and frame controls.
  • Metadata and warning displays.
  • AI-assisted navigation interface.

Testing and Deployment

  • Backend API testing.
  • Frontend browser testing.
  • Integration testing.
  • Error-state testing.
  • Visual validation.
  • Hosted web application and backend service deployment.

The project primarily relies on software-based astronomical data processing and does not require specialized physical astronomy hardware for its browser-based workflow.

5. How is the project creative?

SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer is creative because it transforms a complex astronomical research workflow into an integrated and accessible exploration experience.

Its creativity comes from combining several capabilities:

  • Generic Coordinate-Based Exploration: Users can investigate different regions of the sky rather than working with only predefined targets.
  • Automated Observation Retrieval: The platform automatically discovers and retrieves relevant repeated observations.
  • Integrated Scientific Processing: FITS validation, quality masking, wavelength compatibility checks, and WCS alignment are incorporated into one workflow.
  • Interactive Blink Visualization: Users can visually compare observations across different times without needing separate specialized software.
  • Diagnostic Difference Imaging: Additional image comparisons help users investigate potential changes.
  • AI-Assisted Navigation: Conversational AI makes the platform easier to understand and use.
  • Transparent Scientific Validation: Warnings, metadata, and processing limitations are communicated clearly.
  • Reproducible Investigations: Processing manifests preserve the information needed to understand and reproduce an investigation.

The most important creative aspect is the integration of astronomical archive discovery, scientific image preparation, temporal visualization, and responsible scientific interpretation into a single browser-based platform.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered scientific, technical, usability, and ethical factors during the development of the project.

Scientific Accuracy

  • Avoid presenting unverified visual changes as confirmed discoveries.
  • Distinguish exploratory observations from scientifically validated detections.
  • Ensure that potential candidates require further investigation.

Data Quality

  • Validate FITS files before processing.
  • Consider quality flags, variance information, and invalid pixels.
  • Apply appropriate quality masks.

Observation Compatibility

  • Check detector and wavelength compatibility.
  • Consider differences in observation conditions.
  • Ensure that frames are suitable for comparison.

Image Alignment

  • Account for differences in image dimensions and sky coverage.
  • Use WCS information for accurate alignment.
  • Minimize misleading differences caused by alignment errors.

Transparency and Reproducibility

  • Display observation metadata and source references.
  • Communicate missing information and processing warnings.
  • Preserve investigation details, generated products, and processing provenance.

Usability and Accessibility

  • Make the workflow understandable without requiring extensive astronomy expertise.
  • Provide an intuitive blink viewer and clear progress indicators.
  • Include AI-assisted navigation for onboarding and user guidance.

System Architecture

  • Maintain clear separation between frontend, backend, and science processing.
  • Use modular components with well-defined responsibilities.
  • Support background processing and efficient data retrieval.

Error Handling and Scalability

  • Handle invalid coordinates, missing files, failed archive queries, and incomplete observations.
  • Design the architecture to support larger searches and additional astronomical archives.

Responsible AI and Ethical Scientific Communication

  • Ensure that the AI assistant guides users without inventing scientific results.
  • Avoid unsupported claims about Planet X, moving objects, or variable sources.
  • Clearly distinguish potential astronomical candidates from confirmed discoveries.

Overall, SPHEREx Time-Lapse Explorer aims to make astronomical data exploration simpler without compromising scientific responsibility, transparency, or reproducibility.
